posts.caption:
It starts with a text that looks like your bank: “Did you attempt a payment of $5,000? Reply YES or NO.”

You reply NO, because you didn’t. Then a “fraud specialist” calls. They sound helpful and they know your name. To “protect” your money, they ask for the code your bank just texted you, or walk you through sending money to a “safe” account with Zelle or a transfer. That account is theirs.

Swipe for the real text (as published by the FBI), the script and what to do.

The one thing to remember: your bank will never ask you to move money to protect it.

Got a message like this, scam or genuine? Send it to us at scamdb.dev/report (link in bio). Real messages from your bank or delivery company help too: they teach the check what genuine looks like. Reports stay private.

Share this with someone who banks on their phone.

posts.caption:
A quick rule that stops a lot of scams: nobody real asks to be paid in gift cards.

Not the IRS. Not the police. Not your bank, the power company or a court. Not your grandchild’s “lawyer”. If someone on the phone or in a text tells you to buy gift cards and read them the numbers, it’s a scam, every time. The FTC says the same.

Why do scammers love gift cards? Once you read out the numbers, the money is gone in minutes and is very hard to get back.

Swipe: 8 scripts in scamdb’s US catalogue that end with a gift-card request.

Already paid with a gift card? Contact the company that issued the card right away and keep the receipt. Then report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

Seen a gift-card demand? Send it to us too, at scamdb.dev/report (link in bio). Reports stay private.

#scamalert #giftcardscam #scamawareness #elderfraud

posts.caption:
One of the most common scam scripts in the world, in five languages.

A caller says they’re from your bank’s fraud team, or the police. Someone is trying to take your money, they say, so you need to move it to a “safe account” right now, and stay on the line. The account belongs to them.

scamdb has this script documented in more than 30 countries. The words on the slide come from the examples we wrote for each country, based on police and bank warnings there.

In any language, the answer is the same: there is no safe account. Hang up and call your bank on the number on your card.

Know someone who banks in another country, or has parents who do? Send them this.

posts.caption:
How does scamdb’s check work?

You paste a message. scamdb compares it with 1,199 documented scams from 76 countries, and tells you if it follows a known scam script, which one, and what to do. It runs in your browser: the message isn’t sent to us or anyone else.

What it can’t do: it only knows scams that have already been documented. If it says “not recognised”, that isn’t a promise the message is safe. New scams appear every week. When in doubt, contact the company yourself, using a number or website you already trust.

This is where you come in. Send us the messages you get at scamdb.dev/report: the scams, and the genuine ones from your bank, your delivery company or your doctor. Genuine messages are what teach the check not to raise false alarms. Reports stay private.
